title: Manual tools
audience: Trainee or new worker on the window cleaning (all heights) track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Select cloths, brushes, scrapers, dusters and mops by task, soil, finish and hygiene zone.
Inspect tools for frayed fibres, damaged handles and sharp edges before use.
Apply site tool segregation and withdraw any tool used in a contaminated zone rather than carrying it into a clean zone.

instruction.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instruction.body: This lesson is part of the window cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level, water-fed pole and elevated access work on glazing and frames. Any work above ground level, or from a ladder, scaffold or elevating work platform, is restricted: it needs employer authorisation under a site-specific risk assessment, and the worker must hold any licence the relevant state or territory requires for the equipment used. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instruction.heading: Instruction
instruction.body: Choose cloths, brushes, squeegees, mops and buckets by task and surface; use segregation to reduce cross-contamination.

instruction.heading: Learning goal and job context
instruction.body: This lesson teaches manual tools for routine cleaning work. Start with the actual job scope, site instructions, manufacturer directions and worker training. Never treat a general lesson as authority to perform restricted or specialist work.

instruction.heading: Core procedure
instruction.body: Select cloths, brushes, scrapers and dusters for soil, finish and hygiene zone. Check frayed fibres, damaged handles and sharp edges. Use site-specific tool segregation and reprocess cloths between contaminated zones; avoid dry methods that unnecessarily spread dust.

instruction.heading: Decision-making in the field
instruction.body: Before acting, ask: What is the surface or equipment? What is the soil or hazard? Which product or method is approved? What could harm a person, property or food? If the answer is unclear, pause, protect the area and seek supervisor guidance.

instruction.heading: Worked workplace scenario
instruction.body: A toilet-area brush is placed in the kitchen kit. The worker removes it and replaces it with the site-assigned clean tool.

instruction.heading: Guided supervised practice
instruction.body: Demonstrate correct tool selection and changeover for a kitchen, bathroom and reception area.

instruction.heading: Evidence and feedback
instruction.body: The assessor observes the task and checks whether the learner: protects finishes, hands and hygiene boundaries. instruction.heading: Stop-work rule
instruction.body: Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

procedure: Confirm the job scope, site instructions and manufacturer directions before selecting any tool.
Select cloths, brushes, scrapers, squeegees, mops and buckets by the soil, the surface and the hygiene zone.
Check cloths and tools for frayed fibres, damaged handles and sharp edges before use.
Use the site's tool segregation, so that a tool from one zone is not carried into another.
Reprocess cloths between contaminated zones, and avoid dry methods that spread dust.
Before acting, ask what the surface is, what the soil or hazard is, which product or method is approved, and what could harm a person, property or food.
If the answer is unclear, pause, protect the area and seek supervisor guidance.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence and height notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work at height, on roofs, from elevated work platforms, or on solar systems. Completing it is not a licence, certificate or authority for regulated work. Boom-type elevating work platforms need a high risk work licence in Victoria at any boom length, and in New South Wales, Queensland, Tasmania, the Northern Territory and Western Australia where the boom is 11 metres or more. The WorkSafe WA page (last updated 13 August 2026) and the NT WorkSafe bulletin (no date shown) both state the 11-metre threshold. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. Queensland's definition does not cover platforms under 11 metres (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown). Tasmania's WP licence applies where the boom length is 11 metres or more, and no licence is needed for a boom under 11 metres (WorkSafe Tasmania page, last updated 1 December 2023). In New South Wales and Queensland the boom length is 11 metres: a boom-type platform of 11 metres or more needs the licence, and a shorter boom may not need it in those states. Victoria's WP class has no boom-length threshold, so the licence is not limited by length there. This lesson does not grant a licence. Scissor lifts need no high risk work licence in Victoria or the Northern Territory. Check the licence rules for your state or territory and obtain your employer's written authorisation before any work above ground level.

Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

qualityStandard: Each tool is selected by task, soil, finish and hygiene zone.
Frayed fibres, damaged handles and sharp edges are checked before use.
A tool used in a contaminated zone is withdrawn and not carried into a clean zone.
Dry methods that spread dust are avoided where possible.
summary: Cloths, brushes, scrapers, dusters and mops are selected by task, soil, finish and hygiene zone.
Tools are checked for frayed fibres, damaged handles and sharp edges before use, and dry methods that spread dust are avoided.
A tool used in a contaminated zone is withdrawn rather than carried into a clean zone, and cloths are reprocessed between zones.

knowledgeChecks.question: What should you check before performing manual tools?
options: Whether the tool looks new and whether it was bought from the same supplier as the others
Frayed fibres, damaged handles and sharp edges, and whether the tool suits the surface and hygiene zone
Whether the tool is the lightest one in the kit and whether it can be used on any floor
Whether a toilet-area tool can be used in the kitchen once rinsed and whether the rinse water is hot enough

knowledgeChecks.question: What do you do when a toilet-area tool is found in the kitchen kit?
options: Keep the wrong tool in the kit, since it is nearby
Use the tool from the nearest zone and clean it later
Remove the wrong tool and use the site-assigned clean tool
Mix the tool with the kitchen kit to save space

knowledgeChecks.question: How should cloths and brushes be chosen between kitchen and toilet zones?
options: Use one brush across all zones to keep the kit small and wash it between the zones at the end
Choose tools by soil, finish and hygiene zone, keeping toilet-area tools out of the kitchen kit
Use whichever tool is first in the kit and keep it for the whole working day ahead
Use the kitchen cloth on the toilet, then wash it and then put it back in the kit for the kitchen

knowledgeChecks.question: Which tool practice breaks hygiene-zone segregation?
options: A cloth dedicated to the kitchen bench today
A brush from the toilet area in the kitchen kit
A separate tool for the reception area
A squeegee checked for damaged edges before use

knowledgeChecks.question: What should happen to a cleaning tool with frayed or damaged parts?
options: Keep using it, since it still works for the next room and the one after
Tidy the tool away and tell nobody, since it still works
Remove the damaged tool from use and report it so it can be replaced
A quick note on your phone for yourself and then keep working with it
